content: To make decisions regarding management strategies, it is essential to align them with the individual’s values and preferences. Decision aids can be valuable tools in helping individuals make choices that reflect their personal priorities. Policy-making in this context requires active discussion and collaboration among various stakeholders. The draft guideline document was shared with the External Review Group (ERG) for feedback. The WHO Secretariat compiled a summary of the ERG’s responses, categorizing comments by topic or section. After reviewing the feedback, which primarily involved minor wording changes without affecting the substance of the recommendations, the guideline document was finalized. This publication focuses on recommendations for using dual-stain cytology as a triage test for women with a positive HPV nucleic acid test (NAT) result. For broader recommendations on cervical cancer screening and treatment, including HPV DNA and mRNA testing, refer to the July 2021 and December 2021 editions of the guidelines, respectively. Summary tables of these recommendations are available in Annex 5. For the general population of women, WHO suggests using partial genotyping, colposcopy, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), cytology, or dual-stain cytology to triage women after a positive HPV NAT result. When dual-stain cytology is used, WHO recommends health worker-collected samples and retesting with HPV NAT 24 months after a negative dual-stain cytology result. These are conditional recommendations based on low-certainty evidence. The benefits and harms of different triage options are similar, so the choice of method depends on factors such as feasibility, training, quality assurance, follow-up testing capacity, and available resources. Dual-stain cytology requires liquid-based cytology (LBC) infrastructure and immunostaining equipment, such as an autostainer, along with training for accurate interpretation. It cannot be implemented as a point-of-care test but is suitable for centralized, high-standard laboratories serving multiple screening sites. However, its implementation in low-resource settings remains untested, and it has not been validated for self-collected samples. Evidence suggests that dual-stain cytology may offer better risk prediction than traditional cytology. Women with a negative dual-stain result have a lower risk of precancerous lesions over 3–5 years compared to those with a positive result. However, there is limited data from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and for women living with HIV. No recommendation was made for using dual-stain cytology in women living with HIV due to insufficient evidence. The cost-effectiveness of dual-stain cytology depends on its pricing, which varies across settings. While it may be comparable to cytology in terms of cost-effectiveness, higher costs due to immunostaining could make it less favorable than other triage methods. Long-term modeling suggests that dual-stain cytology could achieve similar reductions in cervical cancer cases and deaths as other triage tests when used in screening algorithms. The WHO guideline will be integrated into a consolidated version for cervical cancer prevention, ensuring dissemination through WHO’s global network. This includes translations into six official languages, policy briefs, and an app. Regional workshops and webinars will support countries in adopting and implementing the guideline. Surveys will be conducted a year after release to assess changes in national policies and practices. Further research is needed to address gaps, including the performance of dual-stain cytology in LMICs, its use with self-collected samples, and its application among women living with HIV. Studies should also evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and equity of implementing dual-stain cytology in diverse settings.
